text:
They Wouldn't Leave Her Body — What a Stranger Found Curled Around a Dead Cat on the Roadside Will Break Your Heart (And Then Mend It)

There are moments that split a person's day cleanly in half: the version of you that existed before you saw something, and the version that exists after. For one ordinary passerby on an unremarkable stretch of road, that moment arrived in the form of a small, motionless shape lying just off the asphalt — and three even smaller shapes pressed against it, refusing to move.

At first glance, it looked like nothing. A pile of fur. Roadkill, maybe, already picked over by time and weather. The kind of sight most people drive past without a second thought, eyes sliding away out of habit, out of self-protection, out of the simple exhaustion of caring about every sad thing the world puts in front of us.

But this time, someone looked twice.

The Shape on the Shoulder of the Road

It was the stillness that struck first. Not the stillness of sleep — anyone who has ever loved an animal knows the difference between a body at rest and a body that has stopped. Sleep has a rhythm to it, a rise and fall, a twitch of the ear at a passing sound. This had none of that. The mother cat lay exactly where she had fallen, her body already stiffened by the hours, her fur matted with dust kicked up by cars that had rushed past without slowing.

She had likely been struck attempting to cross — a mother out foraging, doing what mothers do, taking whatever risk was necessary to feed the small lives depending on her. It is a story that repeats itself in every corner of the world, in every city and every countryside, an invisible tragedy that plays out thousands of times a day and is almost never witnessed by anyone who stops.

This time, someone stopped.

And what they found beside the body was the detail that turned a sad, forgettable scene into something the internet would not be able to look away from: three kittens, barely weeks old, huddled against their dead mother's side as if she might still warm them. As if, somehow, enough closeness could undo what had already been done.

They had not run. They had not scattered in fear or confusion the way instinct might suggest. They had stayed.

Why Didn't They Run?

This is the question that stops people in their tracks when they hear this story, and it deserves a real answer, not just an emotional one.

Kittens at a few weeks old are almost entirely dependent on their mother — not just for milk, but for warmth, for protection, for the basic sense of safety that lets a tiny animal's nervous system function at all. Without her, they are exposed in every sense of the word: to cold, to predators, to starvation, and to a world that suddenly makes no sense.

Animal behaviorists have long observed that young mammals, cats included, will often remain near a deceased parent for a period of time that can stretch from hours to days. Some researchers describe it as a kind of biological confusion — the scent, the shape, the familiar outline of "mother" still present enough to trigger the instinct to stay close, even though the warmth and the heartbeat are gone. Others point to something simpler and, in its own way, more devastating: these kittens had nowhere else to go, and no one else to trust.

Whatever the precise mechanism, what mattered on that roadside was the outcome. Three lives, barely old enough to open their eyes fully, sat vigil beside the one being who had kept them alive — cars roaring past just feet away, dust and noise and danger on every side, and still, they did not leave her.

It is the kind of loyalty that seems almost too large for such small bodies to hold.

The Decision That Took Less Than a Second

Anyone who has ever pulled over for an animal in distress knows that the decision itself is instantaneous. There is no long deliberation, no pros-and-cons list running through the head. Something in you simply reacts — foot off the gas, hands on the wheel turning toward the shoulder, the rest of your day reorganizing itself around a need that has nothing to do with your schedule.

That is what happened here. A car slowed. A door opened. And a person who, minutes earlier, had been living an entirely different day, knelt down on a dusty roadside next to a dead cat and three trembling kittens and made a choice that would ripple outward far beyond that single moment.

The first challenge was immediate: how do you separate three grieving kittens from the only source of comfort they have left, without causing them more trauma than they have already endured? It sounds like a small logistical problem. In practice, it is an emotional minefield. Handle it wrong, and you risk kittens bolting into traffic in panic. Handle it right, and you give them their first experience of a gentle human touch at the exact moment they most desperately need to learn that not everything in this world is loss.

Slow movements. A soft voice. Hands cupped rather than grabbing. One by one, the kittens were lifted away from their mother's side — and one by one, they did something that undid whatever composure the rescuer had managed to hold onto until that point.

They did not fight.

They pressed into the warmth of a human hand the way they had, minutes before, been pressing into the cold stillness of their mother. It was as if their small bodies understood, on some level deeper than conscious thought, that warmth was warmth, and that this new source of it might be the only one left.

What It's Really Like to Rescue an Animal Nobody Was Coming For

There is a particular kind of loneliness in being the only person who stops.

Every day, all over the world, animals are struck, abandoned, injured, or orphaned in full view of dozens, sometimes hundreds, of people who see and keep driving. This is not necessarily cruelty — it is often simple human overwhelm, the sense that one person cannot possibly address every tragedy the world presents, so the mind builds a kind of armor against noticing at all.

But every so often, that armor cracks. And the person on the other side of that crack finds themselves holding a box, a jacket, a makeshift carrier fashioned from whatever was in the back seat, transporting three kittens who, an hour earlier, had no future at all.

The kittens in this story were weak. Dehydrated. Cold to the touch in a way that made every minute matter. Newborn and near-newborn kittens cannot regulate their own body temperature effectively — without a mother's body heat, hypothermia can set in within hours, and hypothermia in kittens this young is often fatal without intervention. Time, in other words, was not a luxury. It was the single scarcest resource in the entire rescue.

So the drive that followed was not calm. It was not the gentle, cinematic version of animal rescue that social media sometimes presents. It was urgent — a race against biology, against cold, against the very real possibility that having survived the road, these kittens might still not survive the hours that followed.

Inside the First Hours: Warmth, Weight, and the Fight to Stabilize

What happens in the first hours after a rescue like this rarely makes it into the highlight reel, but it is where the real work — and the real heroism — actually happens.

Gloved hands, careful and precise, began the process of assessment. Body temperature. Weight. Hydration status, checked by gently pinching the skin at the scruff to see how quickly it snapped back into place — a simple, low-tech test that speaks volumes about an animal's internal state. Eyes checked for discharge or infection. Ears checked for mites. Tiny bellies checked for the telltale swelling of parasites, a near-certainty in kittens who have spent their short lives exposed to the elements with no veterinary care of any kind.

Each kitten was wrapped, individually, in soft fabric — not just for comfort, but because warmth at this stage is not a nicety, it is treatment. A cold kitten cannot digest food properly even if you manage to get it to eat. A cold kitten's organs begin to shut down function by function, quietly, without dramatic symptoms, until it is often too late to reverse. So before anything else — before formula, before medication, before anything that looks like "rescue" in the way people imagine it — there was simply warmth. Skin-to-skin when possible. Heating pads set to gentle, indirect warmth. Towels warmed and re-warmed.

Then came the syringes. Kittens this young, without a mother to nurse from, need to be fed specialized kitten milk replacement formula — never cow's milk, which most kittens cannot digest and which can cause severe, sometimes fatal, digestive distress. The formula has to be warmed to close to body temperature, and it has to be fed slowly, patiently, drop by drop in some cases, because a kitten's swallowing reflex is delicate and aspiration — formula entering the lungs instead of the stomach — is a real and immediate danger.

Anyone who has hand-fed an orphaned kitten knows the particular tension of that moment: the syringe held at just the right angle, the kitten's small paws kneading instinctively at the air or at a hand, the tiny, frantic sounds of hunger finally being answered. It is exhausting. It is also, in its own quiet way, one of the most profound things a person can do — sitting in a chair at two in the morning, feeding a creature who has no idea yet that its entire world just changed for the better.

The Kitten Who Almost Didn't Make It

In stories like this, there is often one animal whose survival hangs by the thinnest thread — and this rescue was no exception.

Of the three kittens found beside their mother, one was noticeably weaker than the others from the very first moment. Smaller. Quieter. Less responsive to touch and to the stimulation that usually provokes a mewing protest from a healthy kitten. This is the kind of detail that experienced rescuers learn to watch for with real dread, because a kitten that has gone quiet is often a kitten whose body is beginning to conserve energy for survival rather than expending it on complaint.

The hours that followed for this smallest kitten were the hardest of the entire rescue. Body temperature was monitored constantly. Feedings were smaller and more frequent, given the risk that a struggling digestive system might not tolerate a full feed. There were moments — and anyone who has been through this kind of crisis with an animal will recognize this feeling immediately — where it seemed entirely possible that this particular fight might not be won.

But slowly, almost imperceptibly at first, something shifted. A slightly stronger suckling reflex during a feeding. A slightly warmer reading on a thermometer. A small, half-hearted attempt to swat at a sibling that, twelve hours earlier, would have been unthinkable given how depleted this kitten had been.

By the time the smallest of the three kittens managed something that looked almost like a real, deliberate stretch — the kind of unbothered, confident stretch that healthy kittens do without thinking — it landed with the emotional weight of a major victory. Because in a very real sense, it was one.

A Grief That Doesn't Need Words

It would be easy to tell this story purely as a triumph — kittens found, kittens saved, happy ending, close the tab. And in the most important sense, that is exactly what this is: a story with a good outcome, which is not something every rescue story gets to claim.

But it would be dishonest to skip past what came before that outcome, because the grief in this story is real, and it deserves acknowledgment rather than a quick edit into something more comfortable.

Somewhere on the side of a road, a mother cat's life ended trying to provide for kittens who had no one else. She will never know that her babies were found. She will never know that strangers cried over her while lifting her kittens gently away from her side. She will never know that her death, tragic and unwitnessed by anyone who might have prevented it, became the reason a rescuer's phone rang with the kind of urgency reserved for genuine emergencies.

There is no way to make that loss into something painless. What can be said, honestly, is that her final act — staying close enough to her kittens that they, too, stayed close to her — may be part of the reason they were found at all. A pile of kittens alone on a roadside might have gone unnoticed, scattered by fear, lost to the world entirely. A small, unmoving shape with three living kittens pressed against it was impossible to walk past unseen.

In some strange, sorrowful way, her body became the reason her children lived.

The First Time They Slept Without Fear

There is a particular moment in every successful rescue that rescuers describe again and again, in almost identical language, regardless of the species or the circumstances: the first time the rescued animal actually sleeps. Not the fitful, tense half-consciousness of an exhausted, frightened creature bracing for the next threat — real sleep. Deep, unguarded, body fully relaxed, breathing slow and even.

For these three kittens, that moment came roughly a day and a half after they were found. Warmed, fed, checked over, medicated for the parasites that had already begun taking their toll, they were placed together in a soft-lined enclosure, piled on top of one another the way kittens instinctively do, seeking body heat and the simple comfort of contact.

And they slept.

Photographs and video from this stage of the recovery show three small bodies breathing in near unison, paws twitching occasionally with the involuntary movements of dream-sleep — the universal sign, across species, that a nervous system has finally been allowed to stand down from high alert. It is one thing to save an animal's life in the technical sense: temperature stabilized, hydration restored, parasites treated. It is another thing entirely to witness the moment its body decides, on some instinctual level, that the danger has passed and it can finally rest.

Why This Particular Story Keeps Getting Shared

There is no shortage of animal rescue content in the world. Every day, thousands of videos and photographs document injured, abandoned, and orphaned animals being helped by strangers, shelters, and rescue organizations. So what is it about this particular story — three kittens beside their mother's body — that seems to stop people mid-scroll in a way so many others don't?

Part of the answer is almost certainly the rawness of it. This is not a polished, professionally filmed rescue with dramatic music and slow-motion reveals. It is closer to the reality of most rescues: messy, urgent, shot with shaking hands, narrated by someone clearly processing real emotion in real time rather than performing for a camera.

Part of it is the specific, devastating detail of the kittens refusing to leave their mother's side. There is something about that image — small, helpless creatures choosing proximity to loss over the safety of fleeing — that taps into something almost universally recognizable about grief and attachment, about a kind of love that doesn't fully understand its own object is gone.

And part of it, undeniably, is the ending. Not every rescue story gets one. For every viral video of a successful save, there are countless quieter stories that end differently — animals who arrive too late, injuries too severe, bodies too depleted to recover even with the best possible care. The fact that this story includes real risk, a genuinely uncertain outcome for at least one of the kittens, and then a recovery that actually happened, gives it a narrative shape that feels earned rather than guaranteed.

People don't just want happy endings. They want happy endings that acknowledge how close things came to going the other way.

What Happens to Kittens Like This Next

For kittens rescued at this age — orphaned, parasite-laden, and without any maternal immunity beyond whatever colostrum they received in their first hours of life — the road to full health is not a short one.

The first priority after initial stabilization is almost always deworming and treatment for external parasites like fleas, which can cause severe anemia in kittens this small given how little blood volume they have to begin with. This is typically followed by a careful, gradual transition from formula feeding toward soft, easily digestible solid food, introduced slowly to avoid overwhelming a digestive system that has never processed anything but milk.

Socialization matters enormously at this stage too. Kittens who are handled gently, consistently, and frequently during these early weeks tend to grow into cats who are comfortable with human touch — an outcome that matters enormously for their future, whether that future involves a permanent adoptive home or ongoing life within a rescue organization's care network. The syringe-feedings, the gentle handling during medical checks, even the simple act of being held and warmed by human hands during those critical first hours, all become part of the foundation for how these kittens will relate to people for the rest of their lives.

Veterinary follow-up typically continues for weeks, tracking weight gain, watching for lingering effects of parasites or malnourishment, and eventually working toward the vaccination schedule that protects previously unvaccinated kittens from the diseases they are most vulnerable to.

None of this is fast or guaranteed to be simple. But for kittens who, days earlier, had no future beyond a roadside and a mother who could no longer protect them, even the ordinary slowness of a normal kittenhood is its own kind of miracle.

The Ordinary Heroism of Stopping the Car

If there is a single lesson embedded in this story — one that doesn't require sentimentality to state plainly — it is this: the difference between a tragedy that ends in three more deaths and a story with a real chance at a happy ending was, in this case, nothing more dramatic than one person's willingness to stop.

Not a trained rescue team. Not specialized equipment. Not extraordinary resources. Just a person, on an ordinary day, who noticed something most people would have driven past, and who made the small, difficult decision to interrupt their own schedule in service of three lives that had no other advocate in that moment.

This is worth sitting with, because it reframes what "making a difference" actually requires. It is easy to imagine meaningful impact demands extraordinary means — money, training, time most people feel they don't have. This story suggests something more modest and, in its own way, more demanding: it simply requires noticing, and then acting on what you've noticed, even when it's inconvenient, even when the outcome is uncertain.

Every kitten fed by syringe in the middle of the night, every temperature check, every gentle unwrapping and rewrapping of a warming towel — all of it traces back to that first decision on the roadside. The decision to look twice at something that seemed, at first glance, like nothing worth stopping for.

A Small Family, Rebuilt

The three kittens found beside their mother did not choose the tragedy that placed them on that roadside. They did not choose to lose her, and they will never fully understand what was lost. But in the days and weeks that followed their rescue, something else began to take shape — not a replacement for what they lost, because grief doesn't work that way even for creatures too young to name it, but something adjacent to it. A new kind of safety. A new source of warmth. A new reason to sleep deeply, to stretch without fear, to knead at a blanket the way kittens instinctively knead at their mother, searching for milk that, this time, comes from a bottle held in careful human hands rather than a body that can no longer provide it.

They still have each other, which matters more than it might seem. Littermates who go through trauma together often show measurably better outcomes — calmer temperaments, faster socialization, fewer behavioral difficulties — than kittens who are orphaned and separated. Whatever they lost on that roadside, they did not lose each other, and in the weeks of recovery that followed, that shared bond became its own quiet source of comfort. Three small bodies, still piling together to sleep the way they once piled against their mother, carrying forward a habit born of loss and now, slowly, becoming a habit born of love.

Why Stories Like This One Matter

It would be easy to dismiss a story like this as simply "content" — another emotional animal video engineered for views, disposable the moment the next one appears. But that framing misses why stories like this circulate as widely as they do, and why people keep watching even knowing it might make them cry.

Stories like this one function as a kind of proof of concept for empathy itself. They demonstrate, concretely, that a single person's decision to care — to stop, to notice, to act — can meaningfully alter the outcome for creatures who have no voice and no way to ask for help in any language humans naturally understand. In a world that can feel overwhelmingly indifferent to suffering, a story where indifference lost and compassion won carries real weight.

It also serves as a quiet reminder that grief and love are not exclusive to human experience. The kittens who stayed beside their mother's body were not performing sentiment for an audience. They were doing what their instincts, their attachment, and whatever internal experience cats have of loss compelled them to do. Recognizing that — really sitting with the fact that this loyalty was real, not a projection — asks something of the people who witness it. It asks for a small expansion of who and what we consider worthy of our attention and our care.

The Ending That Almost Wasn't

Every rescue story worth telling carries within it the ghost of the story that almost happened instead. In this case: three kittens, weakening by the hour on an unremarkable stretch of road, eventually succumbing to cold and hunger beside a mother who could no longer help them — noticed by no one, mourned by no one, another quiet tragedy in a world that produces them by the thousands every day.

That story didn't happen. Instead, someone stopped. Someone knelt down in the dust beside a dead cat and three grieving kittens and decided, in the space of a single breath, that this was a moment worth interrupting their life for. What followed — the frantic drive, the trembling hands assessing weight and temperature and hydration, the middle-of-the-night feedings, the agonizing uncertainty over the weakest of the three, the slow and then sudden turn toward recovery — all of it exists because of that one decision.

Three kittens who, by every reasonable expectation, should not have survived their first orphaned night are, instead, growing stronger by the day. They sleep piled together in warmth they no longer have to fight for. They eat food offered by hands that have learned, through trial and careful attention, exactly how they like to be fed. They stretch, unbothered, in a way that only truly safe animals can manage.

And somewhere, in whatever way animals carry memory, they may still hold some trace of the mother who could not save herself but whose final act — simply staying close — may have been the reason her kittens were ever found at all.

That is not a small thing. That is, in every sense that matters, everything.

text:
The Summer Edition culminated in a Grand Project Exhibition, where students showcased digital solutions, software applications and AI-powered projects developed during the training.

The broader ambition was clear: to support the development of a generation of young Kwarans who were not only comfortable using technology, but capable of creating with it.

Different Programmes, One Expanding Vision

The three summer initiatives differed significantly in their approach.

The KwaraETF Summer School brought together academic development, leadership, creativity and practical vocational skills.

The Ilorin Innovation Hub Summer Tech Camp introduced children to technology, coding and innovation through hands-on exploration.

The Kwara Coding and Digital Literacy Programme offered a structured and progressive pathway into programming, digital skills and emerging technologies.

Yet, collectively, they pointed to a broader shift in how education was being understood.

Education was no longer confined entirely to classrooms, textbooks and examinations.

Those remained fundamental. But the world today’s children were preparing to enter demanded more.

It demanded creativity, critical thinking, adaptability, communication, collaboration and digital competence.

These abilities were developed not only through memorisation, but through opportunities to ask questions, try new things, solve problems and apply knowledge.

A student participating in a debate developed confidence and communication skills.

A child learning bead making or soap production discovered the value of creativity and practical enterprise.

A young person building a website began to understand how digital systems worked.

Another student exploring artificial intelligence began to engage with technologies that would increasingly shape education, work and society.

Each experience offered something different.

Together, they expanded what children could imagine for themselves.

The Importance of Exposure

Not every child who learnt to code would become a software engineer.

Not every participant in an entrepreneurship session would become a business owner.

Not every student who discovered public speaking would pursue it professionally.

But exposure mattered.

Sometimes, discovering one’s potential began with simply being given the opportunity to try something new.

A child might discover an interest in technology because someone introduced them to coding.

A student might develop confidence because they were encouraged to speak before an audience.

Another might discover entrepreneurial possibilities through a practical skill learnt during a holiday programme.

The immediate outcome might be a certificate, a completed project or a new skill.

The long-term impact could be something much greater.

It could influence future educational choices, career aspirations or the confidence to pursue opportunities that once seemed unfamiliar.

That was why learning opportunities outside the conventional school calendar mattered.

They created room for discovery.

A Collaborative Approach to Learning

The summer programmes also highlighted the importance of collaboration in building a stronger educational ecosystem.

Government institutions, foundations, development partners, technology hubs and education-focused organisations each brought different expertise and resources to the table.

When these efforts complemented one another, children benefited from a wider range of experiences.

The result was an educational environment where academic learning could exist alongside creativity, technology, practical skills and innovation.

For Kwara State, this broader approach aligned with the growing recognition that human capital development must prepare young people for both the opportunities and challenges of the future.

The summer period provided a visible example of what this could look like in practice.

Different institutions created different pathways for children to learn.

text:
Beyond the Classroom: How Kwara Turned Summer into an Opportunity to Learn, Create and Innovate

While schools were on holiday, thousands of young Kwarans were learning new skills, exploring technology, developing their creativity and discovering new possibilities for the future.

For children and young people, the long vacation was often a welcome pause from the routines of school. It was a time for rest, play, family visits and, occasionally, the familiar refrain of “I’m bored.”

But across Kwara State this summer, the break from school did not mean a break from learning.

Instead, the 2026 summer period brought together a range of programmes designed to keep young minds engaged, curious and connected to opportunities beyond the traditional classroom.

From the Kwara State Education Trust Fund (KwaraETF) Summer School, to the Ilorin Innovation Hub Summer Tech Camp and the Kwara Coding and Digital Literacy Summer Edition, children and young people across the state spent part of their holiday learning, creating, experimenting and developing skills for the future.

Though different in focus and delivery, the three initiatives shared an important idea: education did not have to stop when school closed.

A Summer of Possibilities

The long vacation created a unique space in a child’s educational journey.

Without the immediate demands of examinations and school timetables, children were able to explore interests that did not always fit neatly into the conventional curriculum.

They learnt through making things with their hands, expressing ideas, solving problems, working with others and discovering technologies that were shaping the world around them.

This summer, that opportunity took different forms across Kwara.

Some students explored leadership, entrepreneurship and practical vocational skills. Others were introduced to coding, artificial intelligence and digital creativity. For participants in the state’s Coding and Digital Literacy Programme, the holiday offered an opportunity to deepen skills acquired earlier in the year and take their learning further.

Together, these programmes offered a glimpse into what a more expansive approach to education could look like.

Learning Beyond Examinations: The KwaraETF Summer School

At the KwaraETF Summer School 2026, learning took on a broad and practical dimension.

The five-week programme, held from August 4 to 25 at Government Day Secondary School, Oke Aluko, Ilorin, brought together academic enrichment, leadership development, public speaking, entrepreneurship, digital literacy and vocational skills.

Implemented through Project TutorED in partnership with She Builds Lives Foundation, with support from the Evergreen Initiative and Saleeman Adedoyin Saleeman Foundation, the programme recorded 204 registrations, 150 enrolled participants and 120 successful completers.

The programme combined familiar academic subjects such as Mathematics, English Language, financial literacy and civic education with opportunities for students to explore practical and creative skills.

Participants engaged in bead making, soap making, arts and crafts, tie and dye and other vocational activities.

These sessions were not simply about learning how to make products. They encouraged creativity, patience, collaboration and an understanding that practical skills could also open doors to enterprise and self-expression.

Leadership and communication formed another important part of the programme.

Through public speaking sessions and an inter-cohort debate championship, students were challenged to research ideas, articulate their positions and engage confidently with others.

The winning team, Cohort B1, representing Bead Making, argued in support of the motion that artificial intelligence and digital tools would improve African education faster than traditional school reforms.

It was a fitting debate for a generation growing up in a rapidly changing technological environment.

text:
I  BET YOU DIDN'Y KNOW ABOUT THIS, AFTER FLIGHT 77 HIT THE PENTAGON ON 9/11, THE FOLLOWING HAPPENED:

A daycare facility inside the Pentagon had many children, including infants
who were in heavy cribs. The daycare supervisor, looking at all the
children they needed to evacuate, was in a panic over what they could do.
There were many children, mostly toddlers, as well as the infants who
would need to be taken out with the cribs. There was no time to try to
bundle them into carriers and strollers.
Just then a young Marine came running into the center and asked what they
needed. After hearing what the center director was trying to do, he ran
back out into the hallway and disappeared. The director thought, "Well,
here we are, on our own."
About 2 minutes later, that Marine returned with 40 other Marines in tow.
Each of them grabbed a crib with a child, and the rest started gathering up
toddlers.
The director and her staff then helped them take all the children out of
the center and down toward the park near the Potomac .
Once they got about 3/4 of a mile outside the building, the Marines stopped
in the park, and then did a fabulous thing - they formed a circle with the
cribs, which were quite sturdy and heavy, like the covered wagons in the
Old West.
Inside this circle of cribs, they put the toddlers, to keep them from
wandering off. Outside this circle were the 40 Marines, forming a perimeter
around the children and waiting for instructions. There they remained until
the parents could be notified and come get their children.
The chaplain then said, "I don't think any of us saw nor heard of this on
any of the news stories of the day. It was an incredible story of our men
there.” There wasn't a dry eye in the room.
The thought of those Marines and what they did and how fast they reacted;
could we expect any less from them? It was one of the most touching stories
from the Pentagon.
It's the military, not the politicians that ensures our right to life,
liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. It's the military who salutes the
flag, who serves beneath the flag, and whose coffin is draped by the flag.
If you care to offer the smallest token of recognition and appreciation for
the military, please pass this on and pray for our men and women, who have
served and are currently serving our country, and honor the memory of those 
who have given the ultimate sacrifice!                                                                                                                                                               

For what it’s worth? My daughter was in the Pentagon on 9/11…. States she saw Marines pushing cribs.

News Flashback

Early 2026

Jan-March

Streaming Wars

The "Streaming Wars" refers to the intense competition among digital media platforms to dominate the subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) market by capturing and retaining global audiences.

As of early 2026, the landscape has shifted from a period of rapid expansion into a phase of major consolidation and a focus on profitability over subscriber volume.

The "Winner" and Current State (2026)

Netflix Dominance: Industry analysts increasingly cite Netflix as the victor. In January 2026, Netflix reported 18% year-over-year revenue growth and is currently pursuing a high-stakes $83 billion all-cash acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery’s studio and streaming assets (including HBO/Max).

The "Big 3": Despite fierce competition, the market is primarily dominated by Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, and Disney+.

YouTube's Rise: Some experts argue YouTube is the true winner of the broader attention economy, surpassing traditional streaming services in total viewership by pivoting back to user-generated content.
Key Strategies in 2026

Consolidation: Smaller or struggling services are being shuttered or merged. For example, Disney recently shut down Hulu as a standalone service.

Monetization Shifts: Platforms have moved away from "growth at all costs" to strategies like password-sharing crackdowns, ad-supported tiers, and price hikes.

Live Sports & Events: Services are increasingly bidding on live sports rights (e.g., Netflix hosting WWE's Raw starting in 2025) to differentiate their offerings.

Bundling: To combat "subscription fatigue," platforms are forming strategic partnerships with telecommunications companies and banks to offer bundled service hubs.

Consumer Impact

Price Hikes: Many consumers are canceling services due to rising costs; over 40% of Americans cited price as their primary reason for unsubscribing in late 2025.

Resurgence of Piracy: Fragmented content and high costs have led to a significant comeback for pirate sites, which some users now find more comprehensive than paid services.

"South Park: The Streaming Wars": The term was popularized in mainstream culture by a 2-part South Park special released on Paramount+ in 2022, which satirized the industry's aggressive competition.

Gold (1974)

Gold is a 1974 British action-thriller directed by Peter R. Hunt, starring Roger Moore and Susannah York. Based on the 1970 novel Gold Mine by Wilbur Smith, the film is set in the South African goldfields and follows a conspiracy by a global syndicate to manipulate the price of gold by sabotaging a rich mine.

Plot: Rod Slater (Moore), a newly appointed general manager, is manipulated by his boss, Manfred Steyner (Bradford Dillman), into drilling through a protective barrier into a subterranean lake. This is intended to flood the mine, causing a global gold shortage and driving up prices for a greedy cabal.

Production Controversy: The film was controversially shot on location in South Africa during the apartheid era. This led to a "black ban" by British film unions, though some crew members defied it to work on the production.

James Bond Connection: Many crew members were veterans of the James Bond franchise, including director Peter Hunt (On Her Majesty's Secret Service), editor John Glen, and title designer Maurice Binder.

Accolades: The film received an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Song for "Wherever Love Takes Me," composed by Elmer Bernstein and sung by Maureen McGovern.

text:
😂Final Days? Get a Grip😂

Michelle O’Neill has declared that the United Kingdom is in its “final days.” She said it in Cardiff, standing alongside the SNP and Plaid Cymru, while welcoming Donald Trump’s casual remarks about a united Ireland.

This is not analysis. It is fantasy dressed up as inevitability.

Northern Ireland remains in the United Kingdom because that is the settled democratic will of its people. Every credible poll continues to show a majority against Irish unity. The principle of consent is not a suggestion. It is the foundation of the political settlement. No amount of joint statements, photo opportunities or overseas soundbites changes that arithmetic.

O’Neill is careful to say she is attending the Cardiff meeting in a party capacity. That distinction matters. She is Joint First Minister, not the sole voice of the Northern Ireland Executive. Emma Little-Pengelly holds the office with her. Sinn Féin does not get to speak for the institutions while simultaneously campaigning to dismantle the state those institutions belong to.

Trump’s comments were exactly what they appeared to be: a loose personal opinion offered during a visit focused on golf. They carry no constitutional weight. They create no pathway to a border poll. They do not override the requirement for majority consent in Northern Ireland. Treating them as proof of “growing momentum” is the behaviour of a movement that has to manufacture significance because the numbers on the ground remain stubbornly uncooperative.

The claim that the UK is in its final days is not new. It has been made for decades. The United Kingdom is still here. Scotland rejected independence. Wales shows no majority for leaving. Northern Ireland continues to return substantial unionist representation. Reality has a habit of surviving these predictions.

O’Neill and her partners in Cardiff can coordinate their messaging all they like. They can talk about constitutional change until the microphones are switched off. What they cannot do is wish away the people of Northern Ireland who continue to choose the United Kingdom.

The Union is not in its final days. The only thing reaching the end of its usefulness is the endless declaration that it is about to collapse. We have heard it before. We are still standing.

#FinalDaysFantasy #UnionStands #PrincipleOfConsent #MichelleONeill #NotInevitable #NorthernIreland #UKForever

There will probably be a lot of discussion about school meals today, but without much knowledge of what kids are actually offered at lunchtime at the moment.

So below is an example menu from my kids' school. Every day there are two hot options, one of which is always vegetarian or vegan. One day every week there are only vegetarian or vegan options (the least popular day for school lunch eating, according to my kids). Quorn is on the menu once every week. There are sandwich and baked potato options with different toppings/fillings.

The most popular day with the kids is Friday when fish and chips and pizza are usually the two hot options.

Gold is a 2016 American epic crime drama film directed by Stephen Gaghan and written by Patrick Massett and John Zinman. The film stars Matthew McConaughey, Édgar Ramírez, Bryce Dallas Howard, Corey Stoll, Toby Kebbell, Craig T. Nelson, Stacy Keach and Bruce Greenwood. News Flashback

Early 2026

Jan-March

Streaming Wars

The "Streaming Wars" refers to the intense competition among digital media platforms to dominate the subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) market by capturing and retaining global audiences.

As of early 2026, the landscape has shifted from a period of rapid expansion into a phase of major consolidation and a focus on profitability over subscriber volume.

The "Winner" and Current State (2026)

Netflix Dominance: Industry analysts increasingly cite Netflix as the victor. In January 2026, Netflix reported 18% year-over-year revenue growth and is currently pursuing a high-stakes $83 billion all-cash acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery’s studio and streaming assets (including HBO/Max).

The "Big 3": Despite fierce competition, the market is primarily dominated by Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, and Disney+.

YouTube's Rise: Some experts argue YouTube is the true winner of the broader attention economy, surpassing traditional streaming services in total viewership by pivoting back to user-generated content.

Key Strategies in 2026

Consolidation: Smaller or struggling services are being shuttered or merged. For example, Disney recently shut down Hulu as a standalone service.

Monetization Shifts: Platforms have moved away from "growth at all costs" to strategies like password-sharing crackdowns, ad-supported tiers, and price hikes.

Live Sports & Events: Services are increasingly bidding on live sports rights (e.g., Netflix hosting WWE's Raw starting in 2025) to differentiate their offerings.

Bundling: To combat "subscription fatigue," platforms are forming strategic partnerships with telecommunications companies and banks to offer bundled service hubs.

Consumer Impact

Price Hikes: Many consumers are canceling services due to rising costs; over 40% of Americans cited price as their primary reason for unsubscribing in late 2025.

Resurgence of Piracy: Fragmented content and high costs have led to a significant comeback for pirate sites, which some users now find more comprehensive than paid services.

"South Park: The Streaming Wars": The term was popularized in mainstream culture by a 2-part South Park special released on Paramount+ in 2022, which satirized the industry's aggressive competition.

News

Gold (1974)

Gold is a 1974 British action-thriller directed by Peter R. Hunt, starring Roger Moore and Susannah York. Based on the 1970 novel Gold Mine by Wilbur Smith, the film is set in the South African goldfields and follows a conspiracy by a global syndicate to manipulate the price of gold by sabotaging a rich mine.

Plot: Rod Slater (Moore), a newly appointed general manager, is manipulated by his boss, Manfred Steyner (Bradford Dillman), into drilling through a protective barrier into a subterranean lake. This is intended to flood the mine, causing a global gold shortage and driving up prices for a greedy cabal.

Production Controversy: The film was controversially shot on location in South Africa during the apartheid era. This led to a "black ban" by British film unions, though some crew members defied it to work on the production.

James Bond Connection: Many crew members were veterans of the James Bond franchise, including director Peter Hunt (On Her Majesty's Secret Service), editor John Glen, and title designer Maurice Binder.

Accolades: The film received an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Song for "Wherever Love Takes Me," composed by Elmer Bernstein and sung by Maureen McGovern.

News Flashback

Early 2026

Jan-March

Streaming Wars

The "Streaming Wars" refers to the intense competition among digital media platforms to dominate the subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) market by capturing and retaining global audiences.

As of early 2026, the landscape has shifted from a period of rapid expansion into a phase of major consolidation and a focus on profitability over subscriber volume.

The "Winner" and Current State (2026)

Netflix Dominance: Industry analysts increasingly cite Netflix as the victor. In January 2026, Netflix reported 18% year-over-year revenue growth and is currently pursuing a high-stakes $83 billion all-cash acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery’s studio and streaming assets (including HBO/Max).

The "Big 3": Despite fierce competition, the market is primarily dominated by Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, and Disney+.

YouTube's Rise: Some experts argue YouTube is the true winner of the broader attention economy, surpassing traditional streaming services in total viewership by pivoting back to user-generated content.

Key Strategies in 2026

Consolidation: Smaller or struggling services are being shuttered or merged. For example, Disney recently shut down Hulu as a standalone service.

Monetization Shifts: Platforms have moved away from "growth at all costs" to strategies like password-sharing crackdowns, ad-supported tiers, and price hikes.

Live Sports & Events: Services are increasingly bidding on live sports rights (e.g., Netflix hosting WWE's Raw starting in 2025) to differentiate their offerings.

Bundling: To combat "subscription fatigue," platforms are forming strategic partnerships with telecommunications companies and banks to offer bundled service hubs.

Consumer Impact

Price Hikes: Many consumers are canceling services due to rising costs; over 40% of Americans cited price as their primary reason for unsubscribing in late 2025.

Resurgence of Piracy: Fragmented content and high costs have led to a significant comeback for pirate sites, which some users now find more comprehensive than paid services.

"South Park: The Streaming Wars": The term was popularized in mainstream culture by a 2-part South Park special released on Paramount+ in 2022, which satirized the industry's aggressive competition.

Gold (1974)

Gold is a 1974 British action-thriller directed by Peter R. Hunt, starring Roger Moore and Susannah York. Based on the 1970 novel Gold Mine by Wilbur Smith, the film is set in the South African goldfields and follows a conspiracy by a global syndicate to manipulate the price of gold by sabotaging a rich mine.

Plot: Rod Slater (Moore), a newly appointed general manager, is manipulated by his boss, Manfred Steyner (Bradford Dillman), into drilling through a protective barrier into a subterranean lake. This is intended to flood the mine, causing a global gold shortage and driving up prices for a greedy cabal.

Production Controversy: The film was controversially shot on location in South Africa during the apartheid era. This led to a "black ban" by British film unions, though some crew members defied it to work on the production.

James Bond Connection: Many crew members were veterans of the James Bond franchise, including director Peter Hunt (On Her Majesty's Secret Service), editor John Glen, and title designer Maurice Binder.

Accolades: The film received an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Song for "Wherever Love Takes Me," composed by Elmer Bernstein and sung by Maureen McGovern.

Charlie Kirk’s TPUSA is sponsored by an Israeli government-aligned outfit; a leaked contract shows

A year after Charlie Kirk’s killing, his organization has buried his criticism of Israel to maintain support from the Israel-based International Fellowship of Christians and Jews. With close ties to the Israeli government, the Fellowship is flooding conservative media with paid partnerships.

One year after Charlie Kirk’s killing, The Charlie Kirk Show is distributed by a federally registered agent of Israel, and his widow, Erika, has reversed his critical positions on the US-Israeli special relationship.

Now, The Grayzone can reveal that the Turning Point USA (TPUSA) organization he founded is holding faith events sponsored by an Israel-based nonprofit with close ties to the Israeli government.

A leaked contract obtained by The Grayzone reveals that TPUSA entered into an agreement with the International Fellowship of Christians and Jews (IFCJ) to sponsor a series of ostensibly Christian faith-based summits between 2025 and 2027. Signed on May 16, 2025, the contract committed IFCJ to pay $700,000 to TPUSA over two years. In exchange, the group was to receive a series of promotional benefits, including main stage speaking slots for its president, Yael Eckstein, and the distribution of pro-Israel "activism kits" to over 200 college campuses.

View the full May 16, 2025, contract between IFCJ and TPUSA here.

Based in Israel and Chicago, Illinois, IFCJ presents itself as a charity that raises money from Christians to assist Jews supposedly suffering from poverty and antisemitism. In fact, it is a fundraising behemoth that is currently on a spending spree, plowing millions into American conservative media while partnering closely with the Israeli government to spread Zionist propaganda.

In a recent interview, IFCJ President Yael Eckstein boasted that her organization effectively supplements the Israeli state: “We’re a non-governmental organization, but we effectively distribute the aid so well that the government of Israel asks the Fellowship to build projects for them during times of emergency.” As an example, she pointed to IFCJ providing “bulletproof helmets and flak jackets” to first responders in Dimona during Israel’s war with Iran this year.

The IFCJ’s contract with TPUSA was inked in the midst of a severe crisis at the house that Charlie built. At the time, Kirk was publicly anguishing over the increasingly onerous demands of those he described as Jewish “stakeholders.” They were threatening to pull their support for TPUSA unless he stopped providing space at his events to conservative critics of Israel like Tucker Carlson and Megyn Kelly. 

“It’s all of a sudden: 'Oh, Charlie, he’s no longer with us.’ Wait a second—what does 'with us’ mean, exactly? I’m an American, okay? I represent this country,” he fumed to Kelly during an August 6, 2025, podcast. 

Kirk had also become an outspoken opponent of US-Israeli plans to wage war on Iran.

As The Grayzone revealed, TPUSA’s largest donor, Robert Shillman, denounced Kirk’s criticisms of Israel at a private gala just four days before his killing and announced that he’d withdrawn $2 million in contributions. By this point, Kirk had rejected a separate offer of Israel-directed donations to TPUSA and refused a personal request from Netanyahu to visit Jerusalem.

The $700,000 contract with IFCJ demonstrates how much TPUSA had on the line when Kirk was killed. According to the agreement, that funding helped TPUSA hold three major faith-based events and will continue to underwrite summits of “believers” and pastors through 2027. 

The Grayzone asked IFCJ communications director Elizabeth Gartman about her group’s relationship with TPUSA. While acknowledging that “we’ve sponsored some things with them in the past,” Gartman declined to answer questions about the contract.

IFCJ is currently listed as a sponsor of TPUSA’s 2026 “Make Heaven Crowded” tour. This tour stirred controversy when a photo appeared on social media showing a giant Israeli flag hanging over the stage at an event at Cielo Vista Church in El Paso, Texas, on August 11. 29. Amid criticism from the conservative grassroots, TPUSA spokesman Andrew Kolvet claimed, “The church put [the Israeli flag] up all on their own. We don’t micromanage churches, especially when they’re gracious enough to host us.”

text:
Michele Guppy offered her response to this seemingly innocent yet entirely infuriating question. It’s below. Why DON’T we “just get a babysitter?” For our adult children with autism. Most of us would hire Freddy Kruegger and hope for the best in our moments of exhaustion.
What do you do for a break? Whether to catch your breath, have a cup of coffee with a friend, a date with your partner, an exercise class or even an Ob/Gyn appointment, which would allow for a brief moment lying down.
Me? I got my daughters on DDS wait lists 21 years ago. Then we qualified for budgets so I am able to pay staff well to stay with my daughters so I can leave the house. For a few hours. Scheduled. Planned. Spur of the moment? Never.
Like my daughters, I too have limited autonomy and agency. Same for most all AofA readers. I can not wake up on a sunny Fall Sunday and decide to pop out to an art show in Manhattan or go leaf peeping in a charming Connecticut coastal town. I can’t go to the Stop & Shop for a loaf of bread unless I have hired staff here. “Hey, how about we….” is not in my vocabulary.
My sister travels at least four weeks a year for a real “get on a plane” vacation. She’s in The Cayman Islands right now. Plus visits to her kids and our Mom in Massachusetts. My brother jets off to exotic places every year. Turkey. Tokyo. A tea plantation in Sri Lanka.
That’s normal.
Our lives are anything but.
Anyone have Michael Meyer’s phone number?

From Michelle, Mom to Brandon.
Sometimes the enormity of the life we warrior caregivers live is so heavy it’s hard to have the energy to continue to speak up – I mean – we have been screaming for decades now and still not one case manager or agency paid to help us – can answer one question for me: Where does my son go when both my husband and I are dead? No family has offered – family who have helped for respite in past, can no longer help as they, as we will be, are too old and frail in what it takes to survive severe “autism” that’s really severe vaccine injury for most.
They have yet to answer that question – nor the absolute tragedy of a simple thing like respite. Read more https://t.co/bKCoh7wEGb

text:
Good morning from Virginia. 🇺🇸

The lights of the Pan-American Exposition still burned over Buffalo when the twentieth century first showed how quickly it could turn. On the night of September 5, 1901, fireworks burst above the fairgrounds and spelled out a greeting for the visiting President: Welcome McKinley, Chief of our Nation and Our Empire. The next afternoon he went to the Temple of Music to shake hands.

His staff had begged him not to. A public receiving line in a crowded hall, they said, was too great a risk. McKinley would not hear it. “Let them come,” he told the aides. Extra soldiers and police were posted. Three Secret Service men watched the line. None of it mattered. Near the front stood Leon Czolgosz, twenty-eight, a brooding former wireworker who had bought a short-barreled .32 Iver Johnson four days earlier and wrapped it in a plain white handkerchief, as if his hand were hurt. At 4:07 p.m., while an organ played, the President smiled and reached out. Czolgosz pushed the offered hand aside and fired twice against McKinley’s breast. The first shot struck a button and died in the clothing. The second tore through the stomach and lodged beyond.

James “Big Jim” Parker, a tall Georgia-born waiter who had been standing immediately behind the assassin, struck him in the neck and knocked the pistol free before a third shot could be fired. The crowd surged in, screaming to lynch him. McKinley, sinking, said, “Boys, don’t let them hurt him.” Then, to his secretary, the words that reveal the man more than any speech: be careful how you tell Ida.

They took him by ambulance from the little hospital on the exposition grounds to the Milburn house. For days the nation lived on bulletins—how much broth he had taken, whether he had slept, whether the color had come back to his face. Doctors spoke of recovery. Newspapers printed hope in bold type. Theodore Roosevelt, who had rushed from a speaking engagement on Lake Champlain the night of the shooting, was so convinced the crisis had passed that on September 10 he left Buffalo and went into the Adirondacks with his family.

On the thirteenth he was high on Mount Marcy, the tallest peak in New York, when a man came up the trail waving a yellow telegram. The President’s condition had changed for the worse. Roosevelt started down in gathering dark. A wagon waited. The ride to North Creek station was thirty-five rough miles through the night. He reached the platform just before dawn on the fourteenth and learned there that William McKinley had died at 2:15 that morning, of gangrene in the walls of the stomach and pancreas, with Ida McKinley beside him.

By half past one Roosevelt was again in Buffalo. He went first to the Milburn house to stand with the widow, then to the old brick dwelling of his friend Ansley Wilcox on Delaware Avenue—once officers’ quarters of the Buffalo Barracks. In the library, toward 3:30 in the afternoon, six members of the Cabinet assembled. Secretary of War Elihu Root’s face was wet with tears. Federal Judge John R. Hazel administered the oath. Photographers were kept from the room. Roosevelt, in borrowed formal clothes, spoke of continuing McKinley’s policy “absolutely unbroken” for the peace, prosperity, and honor of the country. His voice caught, then held.

He was forty-two years and three hundred twenty-two days old—the youngest man ever to become President of the United States. There was no parade, no sea of flags on a portico. Only a quiet library, a borrowed coat, a grieving widow across town, and the sudden knowledge that the Republic had passed, in the space of a single night, from the settled order of William McKinley into the restless energy of Theodore Roosevelt.

text:
Happy Ganesh Chaturthi🎊🥳
Seedance 2.5 Prompt:
All dialogue spoken in English. No dialogue in this generation — vocal music and ambient festival sound only.

Text-only generation, 9:16, ~30s. ~28s render, 15 hard cuts, 4 stages.

STORY SO FAR: None — opening cold into festival morning.

INLINE LAWS

SINGLE HOME LAW — the entire generation stays inside one home and its doorway. Never another location, never outdoors, never a temple, never a street.

IDOL LOCK LAW — one Ganesha idol only. The same idol in every cut it appears. Never a second idol, never a duplicate on any surface.

SINGLE LIGHT LAW — every element in frame is lit by the same warm morning sunlight through the door and the same diya and string-light practicals. No second lighting scheme, no fill from another direction.

CROWD LAW — people are hands, faces, and shoulders only. No crowd counted, no group formation, no repeating same-face figure. Each person appears once.

DIYA STATE LAW — every diya lit in an earlier cut stays lit in every later cut. Flames never go out, never relight.

DUPLICATION LOCK — the idol appears once in any frame. No doubles, no reflections creating a second idol.

CUT + DURATION DECLARATION: ~28s render, 15 hard cuts, 4 stages.

HOOKUP BLOCK — One home. The doorway sits frame-left, the decorated idol platform sits centre-frame-right, the room opens behind it. Rangoli and swept floor at the doorstep frame-left. Marigold strings hang across the door frame overhead. String lights run along the door frame and the wall. Camera holds on one side throughout and never flips. The idol platform stays in the same position in every cut it appears. Every body in frame carries a horizontal position, never height alone. Nothing else appears in any cut. Closed background inventory.

Directed in the style of Giuseppe Tornatore and Vittorio De Sica, with camera staging in the style of Steven Spielberg.

TEXTURE LAW — restrained film grain, atmospheric haze in the light, dust motes drifting in the sunbeams, imperfect real surfaces, skin texture held, no clean digital smoothness.

STAGE 1 — THE HOUSE WAKES (beats 1–4)
Primary hero across the stage: light arriving — flame, sunlight, bulbs, colour.

BEAT 1 — MACRO, low angle, locked off, shallow focus. A brass diya wick catches flame, the flame blooms and steadies, gold light spilling across a pair of fingertips in the foreground. The flame stays small and real. Hold.

BEAT 2 — EXTREME CLOSE-UP, slight handheld drift, lens low and beside the hands. Marigold garlands threaded through working fingers, petals drifting loose and falling past the lens, the garland growing frame-right. Hold.

BEAT 3 — CLOSE-UP, camera low at floor level, pushing slowly forward. A doorway swept clean, a rangoli drawn in bright chalk and colour at the doorstep frame-left, powder scattering from pinched fingers and catching the light. Hold.

BEAT 4 — MEDIUM, camera tilting upward along the door frame. Warm string lights hung across the door frame, bulbs flickering to life one after another left to right, the glow spreading across the wall. Hold.

END STATE: The doorway decorated and lit. Rangoli complete at the doorstep. Garlands strung overhead. The idol platform still empty.

STAGE 2 — THE IDOL ARRIVES (beats 5–8)
Primary hero across the stage: the idol — its arrival, dressing, and face.

BEAT 5 — MEDIUM, camera low looking slightly up, gentle push in. The clay Ganesha idol lifted from its wrapping by careful hands, surface catching warm light, set down onto the decorated platform centre-frame-right. Hold.

BEAT 6 — CLOSE-UP, camera at the idol's shoulder height, slow lateral drift. A marigold garland settles around the idol's neck, flowers resting against the clay shoulders, petals brushing loose and falling. Hold.

BEAT 7 — IDOL HERO, EXTREME CLOSE-UP, camera locked off, very shallow focus. The idol's face fills the frame — the curved trunk, the crown detail, the eyes catching the light of a diya below. Only the face and the fall of light on it. Hold long.

BEAT 8 — CLOSE-UP, camera drifting slowly around the idol, warm sunlight crossing the surface. Ornaments and jewellery placed on the idol, gold catching the light, a hand withdrawing from frame. Hold.

END STATE: The idol fully dressed and garlanded on the platform, ornaments in place, the room warm with light.

STAGE 3 — WORSHIP (beats 9–11)
Primary hero across the stage: devotion — the circling flame, the folded hands, the offering.

BEAT 9 — CLOSE-UP, camera moving with the plate, slow arc. An aarti plate circles in front of the idol, the flame reflected in the idol's eyes, the gold surface flickering with the light. Hold.

BEAT 10 — MEDIUM CLOSE-UP, camera at eye level, still. Folded hands raised in prayer, faces lit by the same single warm source, eyes closed, breath visible in the stillness. Hold.

BEAT 11 — MACRO, camera low, locked off. An elder's hand offers a modak at the idol's feet, the sweet placed, the hand withdrawing, the shadow of the palm crossing the clay for one moment. Hold.

END STATE: The offering placed at the idol's feet. Diyas burning. Hands still folded.

STAGE 4 — THE JOY (beats 12–15)
Primary hero across the stage: celebration — the people and the room moving together.

BEAT 12 — MEDIUM, handheld, camera at child height, wide open. Children laughing, hands reaching for modaks on a plate, sunlight breaking through the garlands above them. Hold.

BEAT 13 — MEDIUM, camera tracking sideways with the line. Plates of prasad passed hand to hand down a line of people, hands meeting and releasing, the plate travelling frame-right. Hold.

BEAT 14 — WIDE, handheld, camera swaying gently with the room. Arms up, dancing and laughing, garlands swaying overhead, string lights blurred across the top of frame. Hold.

BEAT 15 — FINALE, WIDE, camera slowly pulling back and up. The fully decorated idol on its platform, diyas glowing, petals drifting in the air, the lit doorway behind it, the whole home warm and full. Hold long on the last frame.

END STATE: The celebration at its peak, the idol glowing at the centre of the room, the whole home warm and full.

SILENCE LOCKS — no character speaks in this generation. Breath, laughter, and movement only. Every person in frame carries reaction and laughter, never dialogue.

Style: Warm devotional festive realism shot like a film, anamorphic feel, natural morning sunlight raking through hanging garlands, clay and fresh flower texture, brass and gold highlights, diya flame warmth, restrained film grain, atmosphere held in the light. Shallow depth of field on every macro and close-up, deep shadow kept where the light cannot reach. Colour palette: 55% warm golden light, 25% marigold orange and saffron, 12% clay and brass tones, 8% deep shadow. 9:16 vertical, film still not film poster.

Audio: temple bells, dhol and hand percussion in a steady devotional rhythm, conch, distant voices laughing, diya flame crackle, coins and bangles, marigold petals rustling. No announcements, no voiceover, no plain speech.

Nothing else appears in frame anywhere. No subtitles. No text on screen. No logos. No BGM stings or abrupt music endings. No black bars. No commercial gloss, no product-hero lighting, no beauty-shot centering, no poster composition.

🚨Pranav and Karan Adani Offer Prayers at Mumbai’s Iconic Chinchpokli Cha Chintamani

Adani Group leaders Pranav Adani and Karan Adani, accompanied by their families, offered prayers at Mumbai’s iconic Chinchpokli Cha Chintamani as Ganesh Chaturthi celebrations began.

Now in its 107th year, Chinchpokli Cha Chintamani is among Mumbai’s oldest public Ganapati festivals. Rooted in the city's historic mill districts, the mandal has remained a cultural landmark despite decades of social and urban transformation.

Pranav Adani described the partnership with the Chinchpokli Sarvajanik Utsav Mandal as an honour, highlighting its legacy of devotion, unity and Mumbai's cultural spirit.

This year's celebrations draw inspiration from South Indian temple architecture, with the idol themed around Lord Venkateshwara Balaji and the grand pandal recreating the architectural grandeur of the Swarnagiri temple, featuring towering gopurams, deepastambhas and traditional guardian figures.

The mandal's contribution extends beyond Ganeshotsav. With thousands of contributors, it has undertaken blood donation drives, healthcare initiatives and programmes for children, including medical assistance and testing initiatives during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Since 1939, the celebrations have continued beside Chinchpokli railway station, preserving a century-old tradition while remaining deeply connected to Mumbai's evolving community life.

From mill workers to generations of Mumbaikars, Chintamani remains more than a festival—it is a living symbol of Mumbai's faith, heritage and community spirit.

text:
Ganpati Bappa Morya.

On the first day of Ganesh Chaturthi, Pranav Adani, Director, Adani Enterprises, and Karan Adani, Managing Director, Adani Ports and SEZ, along with their family, offered prayers at Mumbai’s iconic Chinchpokli Cha Chintamani.

“We are truly honoured to have partnered with the Chinchpokli Sarvajanik Utsav Mandal. In its 107th year, Chinchpokli Cha Chintamani’s rich legacy has been synonymous with devotion, unity, and the cultural heartbeat of Mumbai,” said Pranav Adani.

Mumbai’s second-oldest public Ganapati, Chinchpokli Cha Chintamani traces its roots to the city’s former textile heartland of Parel, Girgaon and Lalbaug. It carries forward the public festival tradition begun by Lokmanya Bal Gangadhar Tilak in the 1890s. Celebrations have been held beside Chinchpokli railway station since 1939.

This year’s pandal is an immersive tribute to South Indian temple architecture. The idol is themed on Lord Venkateshwara Balaji of Tirumala, with sacred motifs such as the Garuda, Keertimukh, Shankha, Chakra and a camphor tilak. The décor recreates the splendour of the Sri Venkateswara Temple (Swarnagiri) in Hyderabad and Bhuvanagiri soaring gopurams, deepastambhas and sculpted yali guardian figures.

What began with mill workers has endured through the 1982 mill strike and decades of urban change. With nearly 5,000 contributors, the mandal now also runs healthcare and education initiatives, blood donation camps, and community programmes including medical support during Covid-19.

May Chintamani Bappa bless Mumbai with wisdom, unity and prosperity.

His point is that Putin does not need every outcome to benefit Russia economically. He can tolerate Russian costs if the result weakens the United States or the Western system by even more.

Zakaria points to 2008, when Russia reportedly asked China to coordinate a sell-off of American mortgage bonds in an effort to intensify the US financial crisis. Beijing refused, according to reporting by The Washington Post.

That approach, he argues, helps explain Moscow’s wider foreign policy.

Russia has armed Iran with advanced aircraft, tanks and other systems, shared intelligence with Tehran and reportedly transferred captured American weapons from Ukraine for reverse engineering. The Financial Times has also reported that Russia is secretly assisting Iran with ramjet-powered supersonic cruise missile technology capable of threatening US aircraft carriers.

The pattern extends much further.

Russia supplied more than 70% of Venezuela’s arms imports between 2001 and 2018. Cuban and Nicaraguan military inventories remain heavily Russian. Wagner expanded Moscow’s footprint from Libya into the Sahel, while Russian military cooperation with North Korea and China continues to deepen.

Zakaria describes Putin not as a businessman looking for mutually profitable arrangements, but as a nationalist pursuing the restoration of power and territory lost with the collapse of the Russian and Soviet empires, even while Russia itself faces economic, demographic and political decline.

Against that backdrop, he argues that Washington has already offered major concessions: no NATO membership for Ukraine, acceptance that most Russian-occupied territory would not be returned, and limits on the size of Ukraine’s military.

Trump has also said Ukraine started the war and has called Zelenskyy a dictator.

For Ukrainians, Zakaria says, the most dangerous consequence is not another Russian missile barrage.

Generals and soldiers he spoke with in Kyiv told him that losing American support would be the heaviest strategic blow Ukraine has suffered since the full-scale invasion.

They believe they can survive the missiles. What they fear is being left to fight alone.

Washington is attempting to turn years of political conflict over cryptocurrency regulation into a functioning federal market structure.
Senate Republicans have now released what they describe as their “last, best and final” offer on the CLARITY Act ahead of Tuesday’s critical procedural vote. The revised legislation incorporates major changes designed to attract Democratic support, including new ethics restrictions, stablecoin safeguards and tighter rules around conflicts of interest.
The most politically significant concession is the ethics framework.
The White House has agreed to provisions restricting the president and other federal officials from issuing or sponsoring digital assets, while the broader proposal also addresses conflicts involving officials’ crypto holdings and potential divestment or blind-trust requirements.
This matters because the central problem was never simply how to regulate Bitcoin or digital commodities.
It was whether the United States could create a credible regulatory framework while simultaneously dealing with unprecedented conflicts between political power, private crypto ownership and the rapidly expanding digital-asset industry.
The stablecoin provisions are equally important from a financial-stability perspective.
A mechanism allowing federal intervention if community banks experience widespread deposit flight into stablecoins acknowledges a fundamental structural risk: stablecoins can function not only as payment instruments, but also as competitors for traditional bank deposits.
If deposits migrate rapidly from banks into privately issued digital dollars, the consequence could extend beyond crypto markets into the banking system itself.
That is why the CLARITY Act should be viewed as financial-market infrastructure legislation, not merely cryptocurrency legislation.
The Senate still faces the hardest part.
The procedural vote requires 60 votes, while Republicans hold 53 Senate seats. That means bipartisan support remains essential. And even if cloture succeeds, that would advance the legislation to the floor rather than immediately make it law.
This is where the market should be careful.
A successful vote would represent a major regulatory signal for exchanges, brokers, stablecoin issuers, institutional investors and the broader digital-asset industry.
A failure, however, would reinforce the perception that the United States remains politically incapable of establishing a coherent crypto framework.
And that has an economic cost.
Capital does not only follow returns. It follows regulatory certainty.
The country that establishes the clearest rules for digital assets could attract exchanges, institutional capital, financial infrastructure and technological investment for years.
The CLARITY Act is therefore not simply a vote on crypto.
It is becoming a vote on whether the United States intends to remain the primary jurisdiction for the next generation of digital financial infrastructure.
Tuesday could tell us a great deal about the answer.

Dmitri patented a $12 gadget. It still pays him $340,000 a year.

Spokane, Washington. Dmitri drove long-haul routes for eleven years, mostly Pacific Northwest runs, thermos of gas-station coffee riding shotgun.

The trailer hitch pins kept rusting stuck. Every driver he knew fought the same fifteen minutes of cursing at a frozen pin every winter.

So he built a sleeve adapter in his garage. Cheap steel, a spring, maybe four hours of welding on a Sunday.

He filed a provisional patent himself, $65 through the government site, no lawyer.

Three manufacturers said no. The fourth, a small hitch company out of Idaho, offered him 4% per unit instead of buying the design outright.

"Take the buyout," his brother told him. "Bird in the hand."

"I'll take the four percent," Dmitri said.

First year: $600, mailed as an actual paper check. His wife thought it was a refund.

The hitch company got bought by a bigger one. The part started shipping through national retailers. The checks kept coming, quarterly, growing every year without him doing anything.

He never redesigned the part. Never filed another patent. Still drives two days a week, mostly because he likes the radio.

Last year's royalty total:$340,000.

The check still comes. He hasn't touched the design in years.

text:
F-15 Downed Over Iran: An American Account of a 50-Hour Rescue

CBS and 60 Minutes released declassified footage of the recovery of a U.S. fighter crew shot down over Iran in April. Al-Araby Al-Jadeed reconstructed the account: a shoulder-fired missile hit an F-15E, call sign Dude 44, south of Isfahan. Pilot “Alpha” and weapons officer “Bravo” ejected. A ground hunt followed for about fifty hours. The Pentagon has not released their real names.

How the Jet Went Down

The aircraft was on a strike against facilities tied to Iran’s missile and drone program. Bravo likened the hit to a “freight train.” Alpha came down on a largely intact chute. Bravo’s canopy was damaged; he estimated he fell at 70 to 100 miles an hour and suffered a broken back and injuries to an arm and shoulder. The network set the jet’s cost at about $30 million against roughly $100,000 for the missile. Adm. Brad Cooper said U.S. forces had flown some 13,000 sorties in the war, and that air superiority had not removed the risk.

The Race on the Ground

Bravo climbed a ridge of about 7,000 feet. U.S. sources said Iranian searchers came within a few hundred meters. Gen. Dan Caine spoke of a “clear intent” to find the crew. Six to eight hours after the shoot-down, Alpha was extracted in a daylight mission involving 21 aircraft. The helicopters took fire. The force did not find Bravo and pulled back. That night he signaled: wounded, still mobile. The second rescue was put off a day. The American account credits intelligence with deception measures, and bombers and drones with strikes near the Revolutionary Guard to open a path.

The Second Force and the Price of Leaving

Cooper said the second operation put more than 90 troops on the ground and called it the first U.S. ground presence in Iran in 46 years. Two large rescue aircraft landed on a desert strip; small helicopters then flew to the ridge. Infrared footage shows two pararescuers reaching Bravo. Landing gear stuck in the sand. The unit could not take off in the same aircraft. Washington destroyed the two transports—about $100 million each—and the small helicopters so the technology would not fall to Iran. Fifty hours after the shoot-down, Bravo was out. Alpha later returned to flying.

What Remains Political

The 60 Minutes appearance opened a fight inside the institution over revealing rescue methods. Pete Hegseth was pushed to market the story in an unpopular war. Alpha refused the interview and issued only thanks to the rescuers. The account is one-sided, aired by a network that received Pentagon tape. Tehran has not offered a detailed counter-narrative in this report. Fifty hours became media. A cheap missile downed an expensive jet. Getting out cost still more expensive aircraft.
